sentences.text: Anurognathus possessed a short head equipped with pin-like teeth adapted for catching insects.
Studies revealed that the skull was very short and broad, being wider than it was long.
Evidence of a membrane near the ankle indicated that the wing contacted the leg, resulting in a short and broad wing shape.
The animal likely possessed very large eyes supported by enormous orbits, providing high visual acuity in dim light and some binocular vision due to forward-pointing eyes.
Ludwig Döderlein first named and described Anurognathus in 1923.
The species name ammoni honors the Bavarian geologist Ludwig von Ammon, whose collection provided the fossil Döderlein acquired in 1922.
S. Christopher Bennett inferred that Anurognathus was a slower-flying predator specialized in maneuverability, with large eyes adapted for a crepuscular lifestyle.
Research predicting a gape of 1734 mm² for Anurognathus concluded that its prey would have been very small, around 11 mm in length.
Mark P. Witton estimated the mass of a 35 cm wingspan specimen of Anurognathus to be 40 grams in 2008.
Oskar Kuhn assigned Anurognathus to the family Anurognathidae in 1937.
A 2021 phylogenetic analysis by Xuefang Wei and colleagues placed Anurognathus within the subfamily Anurognathinae of the family Anurognathidae.
Ludwig Döderlein originally suggested that Anurognathus was a swift flyer similar to a modern nightjar, a view later challenged by findings of shorter wings.
